intro: Read the deck for the content and these notes for the thinking. Each note says why a slide matters, how to remember it and where surveys go wrong. Work the examples with your own questionnaire beside you, and mark the decisions that have to be fixed before fieldwork.

sections.title: What Surveys Are & When to Use One
sections.big_idea: A survey is a **measurement instrument** for questions you already understand, and it comes after you have checked free data.
in_plain_words: A survey asks a defined sample the same fixed questions so the answers can be counted, compared and generalised. Standardisation, sampling, closed options and repetition each buy something and cost something. Repetition is the trap: fixing a badly worded question breaks comparison with the last round. A survey counts what someone already decided matters, so it does not discover what matters.

Use a survey when you need numbers you can generalise and the concept is well understood. Use qualitative work for the 'why' and administrative data when good records exist. Before commissioning anything, check the Census, NFHS, PLFS and your own HMIS, UDISE+ and MGNREGA records. Remember what a survey cannot give: meaning, the unasked, truth on tap and the missing. **Treat the respondent as doing you a favour**, and cut every item that feeds no planned table.

left.title: A survey fits when
items: You compare groups or track change
The population is too large to ask

right.title: A survey misfits when
items: You don't know the right questions
The topic is too sensitive for fixed answers

diagram.caption: check the fit before you budget

key_terms.meaning: A fixed set of questions asked of a defined sample, so results can be generalised.
Same questions, same way: comparable answers, but the unanticipated is unrecordable.
What a system already records, such as UDISE+ or HMIS.
Existing data such as the Census, NFHS and PLFS.
Repeated interviews with nothing returned, which shows up in refusal rates.

worked_example.title: Pick the right tool
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a team has four questions. Choose survey, qualitative or administrative for each, using the deck's table.
steps: What share of households have a toilet? Numbers to generalise: a survey.
Why do people with toilets not use them? A 'why' question: qualitative work.
How many children enrolled last year? Records exist: administrative data (UDISE+).
Did our programme cause the change? A survey plus a design with a control and baseline.
worked_example.answer: Survey, qualitative, administrative, and a survey with a comparison design.

mistakes: Commissioning a survey because one was budgeted, before establishing that the question needs one.
Reading 'beneficiaries report higher income' as proof that the programme raised income.
Reporting 'share who did X' when the data show 'share who reported X'.
Adding items because 'the donor may want it' or 'we have always asked it'.

recall.q: What is a survey's power and its discipline?
recall.a: Its power is standardisation, and its discipline is design.

recall.q: Name the three data sources and their blind spots.
recall.a: Survey misses the 'why', qualitative work cannot generalise, and administrative data misses who is not served.

recall.q: When is a new survey justified?
recall.a: Only for what existing data cannot answer at the level you need.

recall.q: What can a survey never give you?
recall.a: Meaning, the unasked, truth on tap, and the people the frame and fieldwork miss.

recall.q: What should replace 'might be useful for analysis'?
recall.a: The question 'which planned table needs it?'

sections.title: The Survey Lifecycle
sections.big_idea: Most survey failures are **designed in at the start**, so the first four stages deserve most of your time.
in_plain_words: Eight stages run from objectives to use: objectives, indicators, instrument, sample, fieldwork, data, analysis and use. Start from the decision the survey informs, work back to the finding, the indicator and the question, and cut any question that serves no decision. A good research question names who, what, where and over what period. Decide the unit of analysis, respondent versus subject, reference period and inclusion rule before drafting.

Sketch your dummy tables before fieldwork, so a gap appears while it is free to fix. Treat budget, time and team as inputs to design, and cut items before you cut training. Keep four documents: protocol, questionnaire with variable names, field manual and data dictionary. The lifecycle loops, with pretest, pilot, back-checks and analysis each sending you back. **Errors get roughly ten times costlier at each stage.**

diagram.caption: the eight stages, grouped into six steps

key_terms.meaning: A sketched table of the final report, used to find missing variables early.
The household, individual, child or enterprise that each row describes.
The time window a question covers, such as the last 30 days.
The document stating why, whom, how many and how.
A list of every variable, code and unit.

worked_example.title: What a wording slip costs at each stage
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: the deck says errors get roughly ten times costlier at each stage. Suppose a wording problem costs 1 unit to fix in pretesting.
steps: Found in pretesting: 1 unit, which the deck describes as an afternoon.
One stage later: 1 × 10 = 10 units.
Another stage later: 10 × 10 = 100 units.
Found in analysis, it can cost the indicator itself.
worked_example.answer: 1, 10, then 100 units: the same slip costs a hundred times more two stages later.

mistakes: Starting from questions and leaving the decision for later, so nothing says what to include.
Leaving the indicator definition to the analyst.
Cutting training to protect the sample. Its absence is invisible in the deliverable until enumerator variation appears.
Writing documentation at the end. Reconstructed documentation is guesswork in a confident tone.

recall.q: List the eight stages in order.
recall.a: Objectives, indicators, instrument, sample, fieldwork, data, analysis, use.

recall.q: What does an answerable research question name?
recall.a: Who, what, where and over what period.

recall.q: What does the honest response to a short timeline look like?
recall.a: A smaller sample with the wider margin stated, in place of the same sample with rushed fieldwork.

recall.q: Which four documents does the deck list?
recall.a: Protocol, questionnaire with variable names, field manual and data dictionary.

recall.q: What should you decide now if the survey will be repeated?
recall.a: Which items are frozen for comparability and which are open to revision.

sections.title: From Concept to Question
sections.big_idea: You cannot ask for a concept directly, and **the questionnaire is the measurement**, so every change to it changes what you measure.
in_plain_words: Concepts such as empowerment, food security and trust must be turned into dimensions, an indicator and a question. Operationalisation is the rule that fixes what to ask, of whom, over what period, in what units and how answers map to the indicator. The stand-in always misses something, and naming that gap in the report separates a measure from a claim. The wording, order, options and translation are the instrument, so comparability needs identical instruments.

Groves' Total Survey Error organises mistakes into representation (coverage, sampling, non-response) and measurement (validity, response, processing). Only sampling error shrinks with sample size and appears as a margin of error. Coverage and response bias cannot be fixed afterwards. With a fixed budget, spending everything on a larger sample can starve training. **Ask of every design choice which errors it reduces, which it grows and whether the total shrinks.**

key_terms.meaning: The rule that turns a concept into something countable.
A defined measure that stands in for a concept.
All sources of difference between an estimate and the true value, taken together.
The frame omits part of the population.
Whether the item captures the concept.

worked_example.title: From concept to a number
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: take food security. The chain is concept, dimensions, indicator, question. A household reports eating fewer meals on 6 of the last 30 days.
steps: Concept: food security. Dimensions: access, sufficiency, anxiety.
Indicator: days the household ate fewer meals last month.
Question: 'In the last 30 days, on how many days...?'
Compute the share of days: 6 ÷ 30 = 20%. State what the stand-in misses: quality and dietary diversity.
worked_example.answer: 20% of days in the last month, reported with the gap between concept and indicator named.

mistakes: Letting two teams operationalise 'food-insecure' differently, then comparing their rates.
Treating a late 'small improvement' as small. Price it as a break in the series.
Reporting a ±3% margin as if it were the total error.
Spending the whole budget on sample size and starving enumerator training.

recall.q: What are the two families of error in TSE?
recall.a: Errors of representation (the wrong people) and errors of measurement (the wrong answers).

recall.q: Which error shrinks with sample size?
recall.a: Sampling error, and it is the only one a confidence interval describes.

recall.q: Which errors can be fixed after fieldwork?
recall.a: Sampling (reported as a margin) and processing (if the raw export was kept); non-response partly with weights.

recall.q: What must an operationalisation rule fix?
recall.a: What to ask, of whom, over what period, in what units and how the answer maps to the indicator.

recall.q: What does an extra rupee on enumerator training reduce, and at what cost?
recall.a: Response and processing error, at the cost of sample size.

sections.title: Writing Good Questions
sections.big_idea: A good question is **clear, specific, one idea and neutral**, and its faults are invisible to the author.
in_plain_words: Check every question against five faults. Double-barrelled questions hide two ideas, and the word 'and' is the sign. Leading questions push an answer, and politeness does the rest. Loaded questions assume a premise, so use a filter question to establish the fact first. Jargon belongs in the variable name and not the stem. Vague references such as 'usually' or 'recently' give each respondent a different window.

Anchor every question in time. Use 7 days for frequent small events, 30 days for income, expenditure and health visits, and 12 months for rare events. Recall fails through forgetting, telescoping, heaping and reconstructing from a rule. A spike at round numbers shows answers were estimated. Most bad questions fail several tests at once, and **faults are nearly invisible to the author**, who knows what was meant.

diagram.note: a fourth test: could two reasonable people answer the same situation differently?

key_terms.meaning: One question that asks two things at once.
A stem that pushes toward an answer.
A gateway that establishes a fact before asking about it.
Pulling an event into the window from outside it.
Clustering answers at round numbers such as 0, 5 and 10.

worked_example.title: Run the rewrite drill
worked_example.setup: Take the deck's 'before' question: 'Don't you think you should usually spend more on your children's education and health?'
steps: Leading: 'Don't you think you should...' pushes a yes.
Double-barrelled: education and health are two ideas.
Vague: 'usually' and 'more' have no window or baseline. Loaded: it presumes current spending is too low.
Rewrite as two questions: 'In the last 30 days, about how much did your household spend on schooling?' then 'on health?'
worked_example.answer: One leading, double-barrelled, vague and loaded line becomes two clear 30-day questions.

mistakes: Asking 'Is the health centre clean and well-staffed?' and then trying to interpret a single answer.
Writing 'Don't you agree...', which uses politeness to deliver the answer.
Asking 'how much did the official demand?' with no filter on whether a demand was made.
Testing the question only in English, when jargon returns in translation.

recall.q: What is the commonest sign of a double-barrelled question?
recall.a: The word 'and'.

recall.q: Give a neutral repair for 'Don't you agree...'.
recall.a: 'Do you agree or disagree...' with both directions named.

recall.q: Which reference period suits rare events like birth or migration?
recall.a: 12 months, with the risk of heavy forgetting.

recall.q: What does telescoping do?
recall.a: It pulls a memorable event into the window and over-reports.

recall.q: What quality check can you run on your own data for estimated answers?
recall.a: Look for heaping: spikes at 0, 5, 10, 100 and 500 in a continuous variable.

sections.title: Question & Response Types
sections.big_idea: Choose response formats to match what you know: **open to discover, closed to count**, with careful scales, DK codes and routing.
in_plain_words: Open questions suit exploration and closed questions suit counting. Run open in the pilot, code what returns and field the list as closed with an 'other, specify' escape. Closed options must be exhaustive and mutually exclusive, and collect ages and amounts as numbers, banding later. A Likert scale is symmetric and ordered, usually 5 or 7 points, with every point labelled. Keep the scale identical across rounds.

Rating gives easy but flat answers, and ranking shows trade-offs but is harder, so keep lists to 4 or 5 items. Code 'don't know', 'refused', 'not applicable' and blank separately, and treat a rising DK rate as a sign of enumerator fatigue. Filters and skip logic route each respondent to what applies. CAPI enforces routing and checks, though a hard constraint can reject a true but unusual value. **Every filter is a place where a single mis-keyed answer routes someone out of a whole module.**

diagram.caption: open first in the pilot, closed at scale

key_terms.meaning: Options cover every possible answer.
Options never overlap.
A symmetric, ordered agreement scale with labelled points.
Rules that route respondents past questions that do not apply.
Computer-assisted personal interviewing on a tablet or phone.

worked_example.title: Repair an age question
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a draft asks for age in bands 0-18, 18-30, 30-50. Check it against the two rules and repair it.
steps: Overlap: an 18-year-old and a 30-year-old each fit two boxes, so the bands are not mutually exclusive.
Gap: nobody above 50 has a box, so the bands are not exhaustive.
Better still, collect age as a number and band it at analysis.
worked_example.answer: 0-17, 18-29, 30-49, 50-64 and 65+, with raw age kept as a number.

mistakes: Fielding an unpiloted closed list, which can only return the options you wrote.
Replacing a 5-point scale with a 7-point scale between rounds. The level shift will be read as real change.
Coding 'don't know' silently as missing or zero.
Ranking more than 4 or 5 items, which overloads respondents.

recall.q: What is the productive sequence for open and closed questions?
recall.a: Run open in the pilot, code what comes back, and field the list as closed with 'other, specify'.

recall.q: How many points suit an enumerator-read scale?
recall.a: 5, because 7 is hard to hold in memory.

recall.q: How should the four non-answer codes be handled?
recall.a: Don't know and refused are valid answers to report. Not applicable is structural missing. A blank is a data-quality problem.

recall.q: What does a rising DK rate usually mean mid-fieldwork?
recall.a: Enumerator fatigue, and respondent ignorance is the less likely cause.

recall.q: Why should range checks on CAPI be soft warnings?
recall.a: A hard block can reject a true but unusual value.

sections.title: Questionnaire Structure & Flow
sections.big_idea: Order is not cosmetic: **open easy, ask sensitive items late**, keep order identical across rounds and cut length without mercy.
in_plain_words: A questionnaire has an arc: introduction and consent, warm-up, core modules, sensitive items and a close. Group questions by topic, signpost each module aloud and go from general to specific. Earlier questions colour later ones, so crime questions pull life satisfaction down. Analysis cannot remove order effects. The defence is to put general attitude items before specific ones and keep the order identical across rounds.

Most refusals happen in the first ninety seconds, so open with a household roster or an easy relevant item and never with income, caste or a long grid. Sensitive topics need late placement, a normalising preamble, private modes and a right to refuse. Interview length costs quality: straight-lining, first-option picking and 'don't know' rise with fatigue. Fix variable names at design time and show skips in bold. **Cut every question that does not feed a planned table.**

diagram.caption: the arc of a well-built instrument

key_terms.meaning: Telling the respondent which topic comes next so they use the right frame.
Earlier questions priming answers to later ones.
Easy, relevant opening items that build rapport.
'Many people find...' wording that lowers the threat of a sensitive item.
Giving the same answer across a grid.

worked_example.title: Budget the interview time
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: an instrument has an intro of 3 minutes, a core of 25 minutes, a sensitive block of 5 minutes and a 1-minute close.
steps: Add the parts: 3 + 25 + 5 + 1 = 34 minutes.
Compare with a phone ceiling of 15 to 20 minutes: this instrument needs face-to-face.
Check each core item against a planned table, and cut those that feed none.
Watch duration and per-block variance daily on CAPI.
worked_example.answer: 34 minutes: too long for phone, so cut items or choose face-to-face.

mistakes: Opening with income, caste or a long grid and losing people at the door.
Jumping between topics, which tires and confuses respondents.
Changing question order between rounds, so priming is no longer constant.
Interviewing about violence or stigma without privacy, a matched interviewer and a referral list.

recall.q: What are the five stages of the questionnaire arc?
recall.a: Intro and consent, warm-up, core modules, sensitive items, close.

recall.q: When do most refusals happen?
recall.a: In the first ninety seconds.

recall.q: Which ordering rule avoids asking and then discarding?
recall.a: Place the filter before the module it gates.

recall.q: Name two techniques for sensitive questions.
recall.a: Place late, normalise, offer self-completion or a sealed response, and make the right to refuse explicit.

recall.q: How does fatigue show up in the data?
recall.a: Straight-lining grids, first-option picks and 'don't know' answers.

sections.title: Sampling for Surveys
sections.big_idea: A good sample is **drawn by chance from a good list**, and a bigger sample shrinks sampling error and leaves bias in place.
in_plain_words: A well-drawn sample of a few thousand can describe millions. Representativeness matters more than size, and precision depends on n and not on the share sampled. Only probability methods allow a margin of error: simple random, systematic, stratified, cluster and multistage. Most field surveys are multistage, and ignoring the design effect makes the margin about 1.2 to 1.6 times too small.

The sampling frame is the actual list you draw from. A ration-card list, SHG membership list, voter roll or beneficiary list each omit someone. Over-sample small groups on purpose and weight back. At 95% confidence and p=0.5, about 384 gives ±5% and about 1,067 gives ±3%. Tighter margins, subgroup estimates and cluster design all raise the number needed. **A bigger biased sample is just a more confident wrong answer**, and weights are the bridge back to the population.

children.label: Cluster, multistage
items: Inflate n by the design effect

key_terms.meaning: The actual list from which units are drawn.
Inflation of variance from cluster designs, because people in a village resemble each other.
Probability proportional to size selection of clusters.
Values that make each respondent represent the right number of real people.
Whoever was available, which supports no inference.

worked_example.title: Inflate a sample for clustering
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: you want about ±3% at 95% confidence and need 1,067 for a simple random sample. Your design is clustered with a design effect of 2.
steps: Simple random sample for ±3%: about 1,067.
Multiply by the design effect: 1,067 × 2 = 2,134.
Compare with ±5%: 1,067 ÷ 384 = 2.8 times the sample, which matches the deck's 'about 3 times'.
Plan any subgroup breakdown now, because each cell needs its own n.
worked_example.answer: About 2,134 respondents for ±3% with a design effect of 2.

mistakes: Treating 10% of the population as a needed sample size. Precision depends on n.
Using a beneficiary list as a frame and then saying the programme reached the right people.
Adding a subgroup breakdown late, which leaves the survey underpowered.
Computing an unweighted mean on NFHS or PLFS unit data.

recall.q: What do 384 and 1,067 stand for?
recall.a: The sample sizes giving about ±5% and about ±3% at 95% confidence with p=0.5.

recall.q: Name five probability methods.
recall.a: Simple random, systematic, stratified, cluster and multistage.

recall.q: What does a bigger sample do to coverage bias?
recall.a: Nothing: the missing were never in the frame.

recall.q: What are the three kinds of weight?
recall.a: Design weight, non-response adjustment and post-stratification.

recall.q: What is the standard fix when no good frame exists?
recall.a: A household listing exercise in the selected PSUs.

sections.title: Modes of Data Collection
sections.big_idea: The mode shapes who you reach and what they say, and **cheaper modes systematically shed the hardest to reach**.
in_plain_words: Mode is not a neutral pipe. It shapes who you reach, how long they stay, how honest they are and what you can ask. Face-to-face with CAPI is the workhorse in South Asia: it reaches low-literacy and offline areas, supports long instruments and direct measurement, and costs more. Phone and IVR are cheap and fast, with a 15 to 20 minute ceiling, and they miss people without phones. Web is cheapest and narrowest, and an open link is no sample.

Read cost with coverage. As cost falls, coverage narrows from everyone to phone owners to the connected. A mode effect is a systematic difference caused by the mode, such as more candid reporting of stigmatised behaviour to a screen. Switching mid-project can create an artefactual trend. Mixed-mode designs raise response and blend biases. **Record the mode for every response**, and overlap modes for one round if you must switch.

key_terms.meaning: The channel for delivering questions and capturing answers.
Interactive voice response: automated calls.
A systematic difference in answers caused by the mode.
Combining modes, which blends their biases.
A web link shared onward, with no frame or known probability.

worked_example.title: Choose a mode
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: three projects need a mode. Match each to the best mode using the deck's trade-off table.
steps: A rural household survey with a long, complex instrument and height and weight measures: face-to-face with CAPI.
A quick monitoring check during a crisis with a short questionnaire: phone or IVR, accepting that non-owners are missed.
A staff satisfaction survey with a verified email list: web.
A sensitive-topic module for literate respondents: self-completion.
worked_example.answer: CAPI, phone/IVR, web and self-completion, each tied to its population and topic.

mistakes: Designing for face-to-face and then reading the instrument down a phone line.
Running a phone frame and assuming it reaches the poorest women in the remotest places.
Treating the cheapest completed interview as cheap when it reaches the wrong people.
Switching from face-to-face to phone between rounds with no overlap and reading the change as a trend.

recall.q: Why can a phone frame mislead in rural South Asia?
recall.a: Phone ownership skews male, younger, richer and more urban, so the poorest women in remote areas are excluded.

recall.q: Name two CAPI tools the deck lists.
recall.a: KoboToolbox, ODK or SurveyCTO.

recall.q: What is a mode effect?
recall.a: A systematic difference in responses caused purely by the mode of administration.

recall.q: What does mixed mode cost?
recall.a: Blended, hard-to-separate biases, mode effects confounded with real differences, and complex weighting.

recall.q: What should you budget for in CAPI fieldwork?
recall.a: Spare devices and power banks.

sections.title: Translation & Cultural Adaptation
sections.big_idea: Translate **meaning**, and standardise the measurement: adapt wording, examples and units while holding the concept and indicator identical.
in_plain_words: The instrument respondents hear is the translated one, so translation is instrument design. On-the-spot oral translation is common and damaging, because every enumerator improvises a different instrument. Aim for conceptual equivalence, which means the same concept, difficulty and connotation, and 'depressed' translates by words more easily than by concept. Back-translation catches literal drift, and a committee, field staff and a cognitive pretest in every fielded language catch the rest.

Use categories people recognise: build option lists from pilot open-ended answers and not from an international template. Ask in local units such as bigha, katha, seer and tin, record the conversion factor and convert later. Anchor recall in local calendars, such as 'since Diwali'. Hold the concept, indicator definition, reference period and response scale identical, and adapt wording, examples and units. **Cross the line the wrong way and the state-level total means nothing.**

key_terms.meaning: The translated question calls up the same concept, difficulty and connotation.
A blind second translator renders the target text back into the source.
Bilingual experts and field staff review wording together.
A unit people use, such as a bigha, converted later in analysis.
A list of festivals and harvests used to anchor recall.

worked_example.title: Convert local units later
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a respondent reports 3 bigha of land. The district conversion factor is 0.4 acre per bigha, and a daily wage of 300 is earned for 26 days a month.
steps: Store the raw value: 3 bigha, plus the district factor.
Convert in analysis: 3 × 0.4 = 1.2 acres.
Monthly wage equivalent: 300 × 26 = 7,800, with the 26-day assumption shown.
Keep both the local unit and the converted value in the data.
worked_example.answer: 1.2 acres and a monthly wage equivalent of 7,800, with raw values kept.

mistakes: Accepting a literal translation without testing it with real speakers of the language.
Pretesting only in the source language. A question can pass in Hindi and fail in Bhojpuri.
Using 'employed or unemployed' for people with daily wage, seasonal and unpaid family work.
Adapting the indicator instead of the wording, which breaks comparison across states.

recall.q: What does conceptual equivalence require?
recall.a: The same concept, with the same difficulty and connotations, as the original.

recall.q: What does back-translation miss?
recall.a: A translation that is accurate but stilted, formal or in a tone no respondent uses.

recall.q: Which things stay identical when you adapt?
recall.a: The concept, the indicator definition, the reference period and the response scale.

recall.q: How should local categories be built?
recall.a: From pilot open-ended answers, then mapped to standard categories at analysis, keeping both.

recall.q: Give two local anchors for recall.
recall.a: 'Since Diwali', 'since the kharif harvest' or 'since the school reopened'.

sections.title: Pretesting, Piloting & Fieldwork Quality
sections.big_idea: Test the questions, rehearse the operation, and **check the fieldwork while it is still running**.
in_plain_words: Pretesting asks whether the questions work and uses cognitive interviews with 8 to 20 respondents, while piloting asks whether the whole operation works. Cognitive interviewing has respondents think aloud while you probe comprehension, recall, option choice and sensitivity. Recruit people like your respondents, since colleagues share your assumptions. The pilot checks length, routing, sync, consent and logistics, and passes only when every dummy table populates from the pilot data.

Enumerators carry the standard. They read verbatim, probe neutrally and handle DK and refusals correctly, and they are certified by a written test and supervised practice. Interviewer attributes such as gender and caste affect answers, so match them to the topic and record the enumerator ID. Social desirability pushes answers toward approval. Back-checks and spot-checks catch fabrication and drift while fieldwork runs, and a contact record for every attempt supports a real response rate. **Correct an enumerator in week one, and skip the week-six clean-up.**

nodes.label: Pilot
nodes.sub: a dry run end to end

key_terms.meaning: Think-aloud pretest where the interviewer probes how respondents understood and answered.
A realistic mini-round of the full protocol.
Re-contacting a sample of respondents to verify the interview and key answers.
A supervisor observing a live interview.
Answering to look favourable.

worked_example.title: Size the back-check sample
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a team expects 800 completed interviews. The deck says back-checks cover 5 to 10 per cent of interviews.
steps: Lower bound: 800 × 5 ÷ 100 = 40 interviews.
Upper bound: 800 × 10 ÷ 100 = 80 interviews.
Add a few live spot-checks per enumerator.
Run daily high-frequency checks on all records for duration outliers, heaping and DK spikes.
worked_example.answer: 40 to 80 back-checks, plus spot-checks and daily checks from day one.

mistakes: Testing the questionnaire on colleagues and expecting to find problems.
Treating the pilot as a test of the questions only, when it also tests devices, logistics and data flow.
Letting enumerators paraphrase or suggest answers, which erodes standardisation.
Running data checks only at the end, when the data are no longer collectable.

recall.q: How do a pretest and a pilot differ?
recall.a: A pretest asks whether the questions work (8-20 respondents, probing). A pilot asks whether the operation works (a realistic mini-round).

recall.q: How many cognitive interviews find most serious comprehension problems?
recall.a: Eight to twelve.

recall.q: Which over- and under-reported items are typical for desirability?
recall.a: Over-reported: hand-washing, toilet use, school attendance, voting. Under-reported: alcohol, tobacco, violence, income, caste practice.

recall.q: Why record the enumerator ID?
recall.a: So the interviewer effect can be estimated afterwards; without it the effect is invisible.

recall.q: Why keep a contact record for every attempt?
recall.a: It lets you compute a real response rate, describe the refusers using frame variables and defend the estimate.

sections.title: Ethics, Data & Practice
sections.big_idea: Every row is a person, so **consent, data protection and de-identification** belong in the protocol alongside the sample.
in_plain_words: Each respondent gives time, personal information and trust, and you owe an instrument with nothing spare, storage and deletion limits, honesty about what happens next and at least the findings shared back. Consent is a floor: say what you collect and why, how it is stored and for how long, that refusal carries no penalty and whom to contact. Recorded oral consent to a read script can be more honest than a signature where literacy is low.

The DPDP Act reaches NGOs and researchers handling personal digital data. Its duties and the research exemption apply from 13 May 2027. Removing names does not anonymise: village, age, caste and occupation together can identify a person, and cells of 1 or 2 identify someone. Keep identifiers in a separate encrypted linking file. Keep the raw export untouched, clean in a script and ship a data dictionary. **Choose tools to suit the field team.**

diagram.caption: ethics decisions that constrain the instrument

key_terms.meaning: Agreement given with a plain account of what, why, how long and the right to refuse.
Collect only what the protocol names, for a stated purpose.
Age, place and caste combined that can re-identify a person.
A separate encrypted file holding identifiers.
A table cell of 1 or 2 that identifies someone.

worked_example.title: Check a table for re-identification
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a draft table shows a village, age band, caste and occupation, with one cell containing a single person.
steps: Direct identifiers (name, Aadhaar, phone, exact GPS) are already removed from the analysis file.
Village plus age plus caste plus occupation is an indirect identifier that can single out one person.
The cell of 1 is an identification, so suppress it or aggregate it before publishing.
Keep identifiers in a separate encrypted linking file with restricted access.
worked_example.answer: Suppress or aggregate the single-person cell and coarsen the quasi-identifiers before the table is published.

mistakes: Treating a thumbprint on an unexplained form as consent.
Assuming a small NGO is exempt from DPDP. Size is not a ground for exemption, and research is narrow.
Removing names and calling the file anonymous.
Editing the dataset by hand in a spreadsheet, so no one can reconstruct what changed.

recall.q: What must consent state?
recall.a: What is collected and why, how it is stored and shared and for how long, that refusal carries no penalty, and who to contact afterwards.

recall.q: From when do DPDP duties and the research exemption apply?
Why keep the raw export untouched?
recall.a: So every cleaning step is reproducible.

recall.q: What distinguishes SurveyCTO and KoboToolbox in the deck?
recall.a: SurveyCTO is paid with strong quality controls, and KoboToolbox is free, offline and widely used by NGOs.

recall.q: What are the six takeaways about, in one line each?
recall.a: Decision first, one idea per question, questionnaire is the measurement, manage total error, pretest and pilot and back-check, and care for the person behind every row.

notes.2: Pick your entry point from the table: commissioners read Sections 1 to 3, instrument writers 4 to 6, and field managers 7, 8 and 10. Section 9 matters to anyone fielding in more than one language. The deck says **no statistics background is needed**, since it gives the decision a formula informs.
notes.4: Read the definition for three ideas: same questions, a sample, and numbers you can compare. The table shows each strength has a price. The last row is the trap. **Fixing a bad question breaks comparison with the last round**, so decide before round one which items are frozen.
notes.5: Test your own plan against the two lists. A survey fits when the concept is understood and you need numbers; it misfits when you need the 'why'. The table matches questions to tools. Remember the attribution point: **a survey with no comparison group describes and cannot attribute**.
notes.6: Treat the three sources as partners and read the blind-spot row. Surveys miss the 'why', qualitative work cannot generalise and administrative data misses who is not served. The strongest sequence is qualitative first, administrative data to size the problem, then a survey. **Admin data bends toward targets** because recorders are judged on it.
notes.7: Before you commission anything, look at what exists: Census, NFHS, PLFS and NSS, HMIS, UDISE+ and MGNREGA records. A new survey is justified only for what these cannot answer at the level you need. Even then, existing data gives a **benchmark for your own estimate**. Mind survey fatigue in heavily studied blocks.
notes.8: Each strength in the list matches a claim in the table. Use the table as a design check: '38%, ±3 points' needs probability sampling, 'higher in Block A' needs one instrument, 'up from 31%' needs an unchanged question and period. **Analysis cannot repair these afterwards**, so settle them before fieldwork.
notes.9: A survey measures what you asked, of the people you reached. The table shows how each limit appears in a report. The fix is to describe the number accurately, writing **'share who reported X'** and avoiding 'share who did X'. The people a survey misses are usually the poorest and most mobile.
notes.10: Design as if you must sit through your own survey. Use the table as a gate for every item: which planned table needs it, what decision changes, has it ever appeared in a report? Instruments grow because each addition looks cheap and **the cost lands on the respondent**, who is rarely the person adding it.
notes.12: Walk the eight stages and note where the expensive mistakes sit: most are made early. Fieldwork errors can be caught with back-checks while data is collectable. The deck says errors cost roughly ten times more at each stage. A **wording problem found in pretesting costs an afternoon**, and found in analysis it costs the indicator.
notes.13: Work backwards from the decision to the finding, the indicator and the question. The example uses a cash transfer decision and the FIES items. The test for any question is whether you can **name the decision it serves**. Use a validated module wherever one exists, since it is tested, translated and comparable.
notes.14: A research question names who, what, where and over what period. Compare the vague and answerable versions row by row: population, indicator, reference period and comparison. The deck's test: can you say, **before fieldwork, what number would answer it** and what precision you need?
notes.15: Four choices must be fixed before drafting: unit of analysis, respondent versus subject, reference period and inclusion rule. 'Household member' is the classic silent break. A migrant son who sends money may or may not count. Write the rule and **train every enumerator on it**.
notes.16: Sketch your dummy tables first, then draft questions. The best test for any item is 'which table will this question feed?' If a planned table needs a variable no question captures, you have found the gap while it is still free to fix. Use the three examples as models for your own.
notes.17: The first table shows how constraints push design, and the second contrasts honest and dishonest responses. Cut items, never training. Training is the line that gets cut because its absence is invisible in the deliverable. It reappears later as **unexplainable variation between enumerators**.
notes.18: Four documents make a survey reusable: protocol, questionnaire with variable names, field manual and data dictionary. Write them as you go. Reconstructed documentation is guesswork in a confident tone, and **the person reconstructing is usually not the person who decided**.
notes.19: The lifecycle loops. Each check sends you back to fix something specific: pretest to wording, pilot to routing and sample, back-checks to enumerator practice, analysis to the next round. If you will repeat the survey, **record in the protocol which items are frozen** for comparability.
notes.21: You cannot ask for 'empowerment' directly, so you need a bridge from concept to dimensions, indicator and question. The table lists a stand-in for each concept and what it misses. The gap never closes, and naming it in the report is **the difference between a measure and a claim**.
notes.22: Operationalisation is the rule that turns a concept into a count. It fixes what to ask, of whom, over what period, in what units and how answers map to the indicator. Two teams with different rules get different rates from the same villages, so **put the rule in the protocol**.
notes.23: The questionnaire is the measurement. A changed word, option set, order or translation changes what you measure. Treat changes between rounds like a recalibration: documented, dated and flagged. A late 'small improvement' from a reviewer is **a break in the series**, so price it as one.
notes.24: TSE splits error into representation (the wrong people) and measurement (the wrong answers), with three types each. Walk the table: coverage, sampling, non-response, validity, response and processing. Its discipline is to make you name where your budget went. Most usually reduced **the error that is easiest to compute**.
notes.25: This tree is the memory aid for the previous slide. Two branches, three leaves each. Redraw it from memory: representation holds coverage, sampling and non-response, and measurement holds validity, response and processing. Next to each leaf, write the **one-line example** you would give a funder.
notes.26: Sort the six errors into two families, then read which are fixable. Sampling error shrinks with n and is the only one a confidence interval describes. The other five need design. A report showing ±3% alone **presents its smallest error as its total error**.
notes.27: A fixed budget forces trade-offs, so ask of each choice which errors it reduces, which it grows and whether the total shrinks. The table shows the swap each extra rupee makes. A smaller, well-run survey often beats a larger, sloppier one, and **last round's records tell you which error dominates**.
notes.29: Use the tests as a checklist: clear, specific, one idea, neutral. The table gives a failing and a passing version of each. Add the fourth test: could two reasonable people answer the same true situation differently? If so, the question is **under-specified**.
notes.30: The word 'and' is the commonest sign a question is secretly two. Split each example into separate questions. These items survive drafting because the author has one situation where both halves are true, and they **break on the respondent for whom only one half is true**.
notes.31: Politeness does most of the work of a leading question, and it is strongest where power differences are largest. Use the table's repairs: 'agree or disagree', name both directions, balance the options and delete prestige cues. Put the **full range of answers inside the question itself**.
notes.32: A loaded question forces a false premise. In each example, a filter question first establishes the fact, and the quantity question follows only for those it applies to. Practise on your own draft by asking, for each question, **'what does this assume is already true?'**
notes.33: Write for the least-schooled respondent. If a question needs the enumerator to explain a word, the word is wrong. Keep the technical term in the variable name, and put plain words in the stem. Check the **translation too**, because jargon returns when the translator is a programme person.
notes.34: Vague words like 'usually' and 'recently' give each respondent a different window. Replace them with anchored periods. The second table matches periods to events: 7 days for frequent events, 30 for income and visits, 12 months for rare events. Where it matters, **do both and reconcile**.
notes.35: Recall errors run in both directions: forgetting under-reports, telescoping over-reports, and heaping distorts the distribution. The fixes are shorter windows and landmark anchors. Try the free quality check at the bottom: **a spike at 0, 5, 10, 100 or 500** in a continuous variable shows estimated answers.
notes.36: Run the drill on a colleague's draft. The 'before' line fails four tests at once: leading, double-barrelled, vague and loaded. The 'after' version gives two separate questions with a 30-day window. Read every question aloud and **ask a colleague who did not write it** to find the faults.
notes.38: Closed questions count fast, and open ones explore. The productive sequence is to run open in the pilot, code what returns and field the list as closed with 'other, specify'. Remember the cost of open items at scale: **someone must code thousands of free-text answers** consistently.
notes.39: Options must be exhaustive and mutually exclusive. Use the table as a repair kit: fix overlaps, add missing categories, balance the scale and add an 'Other (specify)'. Collect ages and amounts as numbers and band them in analysis, because **banding in the instrument loses information forever**.
notes.40: A Likert scale is symmetric and ordered, with every point labelled. The table fixes the conventions: 5 or 7 points, labels on all points, balance and constant direction. Likert data is ordinal, so an average from a single home-made item says little. **Reverse a few items with care**, since they translate poorly.
notes.41: Choose by how the question is delivered. A labelled 5-point scale read aloud usually travels best, because 7 points are hard to hold in memory. Keep a midpoint where neutral is a real position. Whatever you choose, **keep it identical across rounds**, or a level shift will read as real change.
notes.42: Rating is easy and can make everything 'good', while ranking shows trade-offs but is harder. Cap ranking lists at 4 or 5 items. If you need priorities, rank a short list and **read only the top one or two positions**, which respondents discriminate reliably.
notes.43: Treat four codes as four different things. Don't know and refused are valid answers to report. Not applicable is structural missing, and blank is a data-quality problem. A rising DK rate mid-fieldwork usually means **enumerator fatigue**, so a supervisor can watch it daily.
notes.44: Filters route each respondent to what applies. The pipeline: ask the gateway question, skip the module on 'no', ask the detail on 'yes'. Each filter is a place where one mis-keyed answer routes someone out of a whole module. **Test filters hardest in the pilot**, because the error is silent and total.
notes.45: CAPI enforces routing and runs checks on the doorstep, which paper cannot. It adds its own errors: a hard constraint can reject a true but unusual value. Set **range checks as soft warnings** wherever a legitimate outlier is possible. Timestamps, GPS and same-day sync also support back-checks.
notes.47: Follow the five stages: intro and consent, warm-up, core, sensitive and close. The table says what each stage is for and how long it lasts. Do not rush the close. A respondent who knows what happens next and **who to contact** is one who will answer the next round.
notes.48: The map shows one instrument as a flow: consent (with a refusal exit), warm-up, a filter on farming, then either the agriculture module or a skip, the core, the sensitive block and the close. Draw the same map for your own instrument and check that **every branch rejoins the main path**.
notes.49: Group questions by topic, signpost each module and move from general to specific. Keep the same scale within a block. The table gives a reason for each rule. Saying 'Now I will ask about your work' is not padding: it tells the respondent **which frame to answer in**.
notes.50: Earlier questions colour later answers: crime questions pull life satisfaction down. Analysis cannot remove order effects. The defences are to ask general attitude items before specific ones and to **keep the order identical across rounds** and arms.
notes.51: Open with easy, relevant questions and save income and caste for later. The table lists good openers and bad ones. Most refusals happen in the first ninety seconds. What you ask there decides **whether the interview happens at all**.
notes.52: Four techniques lower the threat of sensitive items: late placement, normalising, private modes and an explicit right to refuse. For violence, stigma or illegal activity, follow established protocols: private setting, matched interviewer, referral list and **no interview if privacy cannot be secured**.
notes.53: The chart is illustrative: quality falls as the interview lengthens. Fatigue shows as straight-lining, first-option picking and 'don't know'. Cut every question that does not feed a planned table, and watch **duration and per-block variance daily**, both of which CAPI records free.
notes.54: Layout is part of measurement. Use the table as a design brief: fixed variable names in the instrument, visibly distinct enumerator instructions, bold skip instructions at the branching question and one idea per CAPI screen. Naming variables at design time **prevents the mismatch** between questionnaire, export and dictionary.
notes.56: Representativeness matters more than size. The table corrects three beliefs: precision depends on n and not on the share sampled, a bigger biased sample is more confidently wrong, and surveying whoever is available is a convenience sample. **The sampling fraction rarely matters** at development-survey scale.
notes.57: Only probability sampling supports a margin of error and legitimate generalisation. Read the first table for use and the second for failure. Most field surveys are multi-stage, and ignoring the design effect makes the margin of error about **1.2 to 1.6 times too small**.
notes.58: The frame is the weak link: whoever it omits, you cannot reach. The table shows what each common frame systematically leaves out. A beneficiary list is the most tempting and the most dangerous, since it **cannot support a statement about the population**. Where no good frame exists, do a household listing.
notes.59: To estimate a small subgroup, over-sample it on purpose, then weight back. Decide whether your analysis needs districts equal or persons equal, since you cannot have both. **Record the over-sampling** and undo it in analysis, or a deliberate choice becomes a bias.
notes.60: The chart shows margin of error falling as sample size rises. Remember two landmarks at 95% confidence and p=0.5: about 384 for ±5% and about 1,067 for ±3%. Halving the error roughly quadruples the sample, and **clustering means you inflate by the design effect** before quoting a margin.
notes.61: Four things move the number you need: a tighter margin, subgroup estimates, small changes and cluster design. The cost table gives rules of thumb, such as about 3 times the sample for ±3% instead of ±5%. Most underpowered surveys got there when **a subgroup breakdown was added late**.
notes.62: Sample size shrinks sampling error and nothing else. Coverage, non-response and selection bias stay however large n grows. The Literary Digest example shows it: 2.4 million responses and the wrong answer. Remember: **size is a precision instrument and gives no accuracy**.
notes.63: Weights make each respondent stand for the right number of real people. Three kinds appear: design weights, non-response adjustment and post-stratification. Plan for them at the design stage. An unweighted mean on NFHS or PLFS data is **wrong twice**: the level and the standard error.
notes.65: Mode shapes who you reach, how long they stay, how honest they are and what you can ask. Choose the mode before you write questions, because an instrument built for face-to-face rarely survives being read down a phone line. Use the table to **match mode to topic and length**.
notes.66: Face-to-face with CAPI is the workhorse: it reaches low-literacy and offline areas, handles long instruments and measures height, weight and GPS. Costs are travel, staff and device logistics. Budget spare devices and power banks. An enumerator **consistently 40% faster than the team** deserves a check.
notes.67: Phone and IVR are cheap and fast and must be short, with 15 to 20 minutes as the ceiling. Phone ownership skews male, younger and richer, so the frame excludes the poorest women, and nothing in the data shows it. The table lists who answers and who is missed. **Check the skew** before you rely on a phone sample.
notes.68: Web has the lowest cost and the narrowest coverage. It suits staff, students and professionals, and fails for rural populations. An open link has no frame, no known selection probability and no way to weight. It **describes respondents only**, with nothing to say about a population.
notes.69: Compare four modes by cost, coverage, length and best use. There is no best mode, only the right trade-off for your population, budget, topic and timeline. Always **read cost beside coverage**: the cheapest completed interview is not cheap if it reaches the wrong people.
notes.70: The chart is illustrative: as cost falls, coverage narrows from everyone to phone owners to the connected. Cheaper modes shed the hardest to reach. The line at the bottom is the one to remember: **the people excluded are usually the subject of the survey**.
notes.71: A mode effect is a systematic difference caused by the mode. Stigmatised behaviour comes out more truthfully to a screen, and approved behaviour is over-reported to a person. A mid-project switch from face-to-face to phone can create a trend that is pure artefact. If you must switch, **overlap the modes for one round**.
notes.72: Mixed-mode designs raise response and cut cost and also blend biases. Record the mode on every response so you can test for mode effects. A single pooled figure with no check is where these designs go wrong. Test for mode effects **before you pool**.
notes.74: A single instrument is rarely enough in a multilingual setting. The translated version is the instrument respondents hear, so translation is design. The worst case is on-the-spot oral translation: every enumerator improvises a different instrument and **no record of it exists**.
notes.75: Aim for conceptual equivalence. The table gives four tests: semantic, conceptual, difficulty and connotation. 'Empowered' has no clean equivalent in many languages, so adapt to a locally meaningful idea. 'Depressed' translates words well and concepts rarely, which is why **validated instruments exist** in Indian languages.
notes.76: Follow the four steps: forward translation, blind back-translation, comparison and reconciliation. It catches literal drift well. It misses a translation that is accurate but stilted or in a tone no respondent uses, and that is **the commoner failure**.
notes.77: Combine methods. Back-translation catches literal errors, a committee catches tone and fit, field staff catch what is sayable aloud and a cognitive pretest shows how respondents interpret it. Run the pretest **in every fielded language**, since a question can pass in Hindi and fail in Bhojpuri.
notes.78: Imported categories misfit local reality. Compare each row: 'employed or unemployed' against daily wage, seasonal and unpaid family work, or monthly income bands against pay by the day or at harvest. Build option lists **from pilot open-ended answers**, then map to standard categories in analysis, keeping both.
notes.79: Ask in the units people use and convert later. Record the local unit, the conversion factor and the raw value. Land units vary by district, so key a **conversion table to location** inside the CAPI form. Forcing mental conversion adds error.
notes.80: A local events calendar sharpens recall. 'Since Diwali' or 'since the kharif harvest' is vivid, and 'last 12 months' is abstract. Build the calendar during the pilot with local staff and print it in the field manual. This is **one of the cheapest accuracy gains** in survey design.
notes.81: Adapt the wording, examples and units; hold the concept, indicator definition, reference period and response scale identical. That is what keeps a survey locally meaningful and nationally comparable. Cross the line the wrong way, **adapting the indicator and keeping the wording**, and the state total means nothing.
notes.83: Separate two checks. Pretesting asks whether the questions work, with 8 to 20 respondents and probing. Piloting asks whether the whole operation works, in a realistic mini-round. Skipping either is the costliest false economy. Pretest first, **revise, then pilot**, and lock the instrument last.
notes.84: Cognitive interviewing asks respondents to think aloud while you probe how they understood and answered. The four probes in the table cover comprehension, recall, option choice and sensitivity. Recruit people who look like your respondents. **Testing on colleagues finds nothing**, because they share your assumptions.
notes.85: The pilot tests the system: length, routing, devices, sync, logistics, consent and data flow. The table gives pass conditions. The final check is the important one: run pilot data through your analysis scripts and see whether **every dummy table populates** while there is time to fix it.
notes.86: Standardised training makes 'the same question asked the same way' true. Read questions verbatim, probe neutrally, handle DK and refusals correctly and practise with role-plays. Certify only after a written test and a supervised practice interview, since it is **the cheapest point to identify** who cannot do the job.
notes.87: Interviewers shape answers through gender, caste, age and manner. Match the interviewer to the topic where it matters, such as a woman enumerator for violence or reproductive health. Record the **enumerator ID on every interview**, or the effect cannot be estimated afterwards.
notes.88: People over-report approved behaviour and under-report stigmatised behaviour. Use the mitigations: normalising preambles, private self-completion, assured confidentiality, questions about behaviour and not identity. Where you can, **validate against something observed**, such as a soap-and-water check at the handwashing station.
notes.89: Back-checks re-contact respondents, and spot-checks observe live interviews. The table gives sample sizes and what each catches, plus daily high-frequency checks. They only work while fieldwork runs, so **start the daily checks on day one** and correct an enumerator in week one and avoid discarding week-six data.
notes.90: Non-response bites when non-responders differ from responders. Make repeat visits at different times, track the full response rate, compare responders to the frame and adjust with weights. Keep a **contact record for every attempt**: it lets you compute a real response rate and describe the refusers.
notes.92: Every row is a person who gave you time and trust. The table pairs each thing they give with what you owe. The last row is the commitment to keep: at minimum, share findings back. Communities notice when nothing returns, and **falling response rates are an ethics problem and a quality problem**.
notes.93: Consent is a floor. State what you collect and why, how it is stored and for how long, that refusal carries no penalty and whom to contact. A thumbprint on an unexplained form is not consent. Where literacy is low, **recorded oral consent to a read script** can be more honest than a signature.
notes.94: The DPDP Act reaches NGOs and researchers who handle personal digital data, including CAPI surveys. The duties and the research exemption apply from 13 May 2027. Size is no ground for exemption, and research is a narrow one. Treat the table as a protocol checklist and **get sensitive or children's data reviewed**.
notes.95: Removing names is not enough. Village, age, caste and occupation together can single out one person, and GPS makes it worse. Keep identifiers in a separate encrypted linking file and work from a de-identified file. **Suppress or aggregate small cells** before publishing, since a cell of 1 or 2 identifies someone.
notes.96: A survey is done when someone else can open the documented dataset and understand every column. Use the table: validation in the form, raw export untouched, cleaning in a script and a data dictionary. Spreadsheet edits by hand are where **a dataset stops being reproducible**.
notes.97: Four tools appear in the first table and a different fit in the second: KoboToolbox, ODK, SurveyCTO and Survey Solutions, plus CSPro for census-style operations. Choose for the field team. The right tool works offline **on the devices you own**, with a support person you can reach.
notes.98: Use the reading list in a sensible order. Groves covers TSE in full, Fowler covers question wording, Bradburn, Sudman and Wansink give worked examples. The last row is the fastest lesson: **read a live national instrument beside its report** and trace each table to a numbered question.
notes.99: Six takeaways, and the second table says what each rules out. Test your next survey against them. The closing line is the encouragement: none needs a bigger budget, and all need **decisions taken before fieldwork**, the only time most survey errors can still be prevented.
